title: Does recursively splitting a splay tree always take linear total time?
formal: Start with an arbitrary n-node binary search tree. A split operation receives a current component tree and a key x in it, searches for x, splays x to that component’s root, and deletes x, leaving its left and right subtrees as separate components. Is the total cost of every legal sequence of n splits O(n)? Count all searches, rotations, and constant-time component bookkeeping. The input to each operation supplies the component’s root handle; identifying which component contains x is not a separate search problem.
answer_criterion: Prove one universal linear bound for every initial tree and legal split order, or prove that total cost divided by n is unbounded over such inputs. A bound with any unbounded multiplicative factor is partial progress.
context:
Ordinary search adjusts one tree and keeps all its keys available. A split removes its accessed key and permanently separates the keys on its two sides. Subsequent operations happen independently in the resulting components. Every original key is accessed as a pivot exactly once, but it can participate in rotations caused by earlier pivots.

For example, splitting at the median key first separates the two halves of the key order. Continuing recursively with medians gives a balanced pattern of subproblems. Another legal sequence repeatedly chooses an extreme key and leaves almost the entire tree in one component. The conjecture must cover both, including mixtures chosen from different components.

There are only n requested pivots, which explains the linear target, but not a linear upper bound for the actual implementation. A key may lie deep in the current tree. The proof must show that restructuring work can be charged globally without repeatedly charging the same surviving material too much.

This differs from the deque conjecture: a deque deletes only an extreme, whereas a split may select any internal rank and produce two nonempty trees. The July 2026 analysis gives a new nearly linear bound for this splitting process, making the remaining multiplicative gap explicit.
why: I include this because recursive partitioning is a basic way to organize ordered data. The conjecture asks whether splaying pays only for the number of objects eventually removed, regardless of the partition order. It is a sharply delimited test of the amortization techniques used for adaptive search trees.
definitions: Keys have a fixed total order and are compared rather than arithmetically manipulated. Splaying uses zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rotations. Each key is removed exactly once; no insertions occur. The sequence can choose any currently nonempty component. The bound is a worst-case bound on total cost over complete sequences, not a per-split worst-case bound.

progress.text: Pettie records Lucas’s split conjecture and distinguishes it from traversal and deque workloads. Even the deletion-only extreme-key case captures a restricted form of the deque question.
Chmel and coauthors prove total split cost $O(n\log\log n\,\log^2\log\log n)$ in Appendix D. The O(n) bound remains the target.
